extracted.intended_audience: poets, students, and readers studying Allen Ginsberg's style and Beat-generation poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for composing or analyzing poetry in the Ginsberg/Beat tradition — techniques of line, form, imagery, voice, and performance drawn from this biography and stylistic account.

rubrics_metrics.name: William Carlos Williams' practical advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't emulate old masters; 'speak with your own voice'; 'use strong visual imagery'; 'shift from formal to free-verse.' (Advice Williams gave Ginsberg after reading his early poems.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Williams' recommendation is presented as formative guidance that Ginsberg followed when composing Howl — emphasizes originality of voice, vivid concrete imagery, and moving away from strict rhyme/meter toward free-verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include unedited mental associations ('First thought, best thought')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use unedited mental associations to reveal the mind at work — slogan: 'First thought, best thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Naropa teaching/poetic slogan encourages capturing spontaneous mental flow in the poem; Ginsberg promoted exposing raw associations as a technique for authenticity and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't tell / 'No ideas but in things.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer expression through carefully observed physical details rather than abstract statements — 'Show, don't tell.' and 'No ideas but in things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A core stylistic precept: concrete sensory detail should carry meaning; avoid abstract exposition. This is given as a deliberate poetic principle Ginsberg taught and practiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Whitmanian long line
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the long line as a dynamic technique, following Whitman — long, lilting lines that can sexualize and elevate subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ginsberg used extended lines to produce epic/free-verse effects (emotional intensity, cadence, breath-driven phrasing). The long line underpins thematic passion (e.g., American democracy, erotic experience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anaphora / repetition of a fixed base
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ repetition/anaphora (a fixed base word or phrase) — examples: 'who' in Howl, 'America' in 'America'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anaphora is a recognizable Ginsbergian device to build momentum and emphasis; the page notes it was useful early on but can function as a 'crutch' indicating lack of confidence and was later largely abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eyeball kick — juxtapose starkly contrasting images
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an 'eyeball kick' by placing two contrasting images or elements together (e.g., something weak with something strong; high culture with low culture) — phrase derived from Cézanne/haiku observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique produces a visual/spiritual jolt in the reader; examples include neologisms like 'hydrogen jukebox.' It is explicitly tied to haiku contrast and Cézanne's color-contrast effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting experiments: stepped triadic lines and visual layout
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with line-and-page formatting (e.g., the 'stepped triadic' format reminiscent of William Carlos Williams), using visual layout as part of poetic technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ginsberg tried and later abandoned some formats (stepped triadic) after developing other techniques (long line), but such experiments reappear strategically (e.g., travelogues in The Fall of America). Use formatting deliberately for pacing and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural organization: inverted-pyramid composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize long poems as inverted pyramids, where larger sections lead to smaller sections (noted for Howl and Kaddish).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a structural strategy for building scope and then narrowing focus; useful in expansive free-verse narratives to manage momentum and thematic development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line-length variation: mix long and short lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary line lengths within a poem (mix of longer and shorter lines) as an expressive device (noted particularly in 'America').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternating line lengths can create contrast, rhythm shifts, tonal variation, and structural interest; use consciously to modulate pace and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate music and rhythm; collaborate with musicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate musical elements into poetry (compose tunes, use harmonium, set poems to music, collaborate with composers like Philip Glass).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ginsberg frequently performed with musical accompaniment and recorded songs/albums. Thinking musically about cadence and sound can shape lineation, repetition, and performance practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuse the personal with the political
rubrics_metrics.description: Use intimate/personal material (biography, family, mental illness) alongside political/social critique — personal aspects can be as important as political ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ginsberg's work interweaves sympathy for individuals (e.g., Carl Solomon, his mother) with broader attacks on societal systems ('Moloch'). This fusion gives emotional weight and moral urgency to poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision as craft (not pure spontaneity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Value revision: Ginsberg was 'much more prone to revise than Kerouac' — spontaneous material is often edited and shaped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although spontaneity is a source of raw material, the finished poem may undergo substantial revision. Treat initial improvisation as a draft to be honed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt and synthesize diverse influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately draw on broad influences (Modernism, Romanticism, jazz cadence, Buddhist practice, haiku, Cézanne, Surrealism) and adapt techniques to your voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ginsberg's style is a synthesis of many traditions; study and selectively appropriate techniques (visual imagery from Blake/Whitman, jazz rhythm, Buddhist attention) rather than copying wholesale.
